territorial_scope.description: Illinois state statute; the Attorney General enforces it against developers, and the text sets no express geographic limit on developers' activities.

evidence.quote: The Attorney General may bring a civil action against a developer that violates Sections 15 or 25.

summary.short: Introduced Illinois bill (Artificial Intelligence Safety and Security Protocol Act) requiring developers of foundation models trained with compute costing at least $100,000,000 to publish a safety and security protocol, publish risk assessment reports every 90 days and undergo annual third-party audits; civil penalties up to $1,000,000.
summary.long: Introduced bill in the 104th Illinois General Assembly (HB3506) that would create the Artificial Intelligence Safety and Security Protocol Act. It applies to a 'developer', defined as a person that has trained at least one foundation model with compute costing at least $100,000,000 at prevailing cloud computing prices. Developers would have to produce, implement, follow and conspicuously publish a safety and security protocol covering critical risks, including chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear weapons, cyber-attacks and evasion of control by the model; material modifications must be published within 30 days. No less than every 90 days, developers must publish a risk assessment report, and must retain specific test records for at least 5 years. Developers may redact documents for trade secret, public safety or national security reasons, must keep unredacted versions for 5 years and allow Attorney General inspection. At least once every calendar year, a developer must retain a reputable third-party auditor and publish the audit report within 90 days after completion. Whistleblower Act protections apply, and developers must provide an anonymous internal disclosure process. The Attorney General may bring civil actions for violations of Sections 15 or 25, with civil penalties up to $1,000,000, and may seek injunctive relief. The text states no effective date.

notes: Bill as introduced; no effective date is stated, although Section 15(a) refers to 'the effective date'. The Employee definition uses 'covered models' and 'covered model derivatives', which are not defined; the rest of the text uses 'foundation model'. The Employee definition refers to 'critical harm' while Sections 15, 30 and 35 use 'critical risk'. Section 25(a)(3) refers to possible violations of Section 20, but Section 35(a) provides civil penalties only for violations of Sections 15 or 25. Section 30(a) bars criminal penalties under the Whistleblower Act for certain disclosures, but that Act is not identified by citation. Section 5 and Section 10 contain no operative obligations.

thresholds.variable_text: persons who suffer death or serious injury from a critical risk
thresholds.measurement: Not specified in the text. Applies to a foreseeable and non-trivial risk that a developer's development, storage or deployment of a foundation model will result in the harm.
thresholds.consequence: Defines 'critical risk', on which the safety and security protocol, risk assessment report, audit and related duties depend.
thresholds.conditions: Harm must fall within one of four listed routes: CBRN weapon creation and release, cyber-attack, qualifying criminal conduct with limited human intervention, or evading control of the developer or user.

evidence.quote: the death of, or serious injury to, more than 100 people

thresholds.variable_text: damage to rights in money or property from a critical risk
thresholds.value_text: more than $1,000,000,000 in damage to rights in money or property
thresholds.consequence: Defines 'critical risk' as an alternative to the 100-person harm threshold, on which the Act's duties depend.
thresholds.conditions: Same as the 100-person harm threshold: a foreseeable and non-trivial risk through one of the four listed routes.

thresholds.variable_text: cost of computational power used to train a foundation model, measured at prevailing cloud computing prices
thresholds.value_text: costs at least $100,000,000 when measured using prevailing market prices of cloud computing
thresholds.measurement: Cost of computational power measured using prevailing market prices of cloud computing. The text states no time window.
thresholds.consequence: Defines 'developer', the addressee of the Act's duties, as a person that has trained at least one foundation model at or above this cost.
thresholds.conditions: The person must have trained at least one foundation model with this quantity of computational power.

evidence.quote: costs at least $100,000,000 when measured using prevailing market prices of cloud computing
